title: Etale chart calculus for derived algebraic-space modules
statement: Let $S$ be a scheme [def-pc-scheme]. Use algebraic spaces over $S$ and their small etale structure sheaves [def-trf-algebraic-space], module sheaves [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category], and unbounded derived categories [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Write $D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_Z)$ for objects with quasi-coherent cohomology [def-trf-space-quasi-coherent-module]. The functors $Lu^*\dashv Ru_*$ derive tensor pullback and direct image [def-trf-space-etale-module-functors], using K-flat resolutions [def-pc-kflat-complex] and K-injective resolutions (complexes $I$ for which every map from an acyclic complex to $I$ is null-homotopic). For every morphism $u:Z\to W$, $Lu^*$ preserves quasi-coherent cohomology. If $a:V\to W$ is etale, put $Z_V=Z\times_WV$, with $b:Z_V\to Z$ and $u_V:Z_V\to V$. There are canonical isomorphisms $a^*Ru_*K\cong R(u_V)_*b^*K$ for every $K\in D(\mathcal O_Z)$ and $b^*Lu^*L\cong Lu_V^*a^*L$ for every $L\in D(\mathcal O_W)$. Etale pullback here is exact restriction to the slice site. Having quasi-coherent cohomology can be checked on the restrictions to a jointly surjective etale scheme covering. Derived pullbacks have their canonical associative and unital composition isomorphisms; derived pushforward composition is the right-adjoint conjugate of pullback composition, so these comparisons respect units and counits.

proof.text: Work in the enlarged etale ringed sites $\mathcal C_Z$ of the cited model, all small relative to the module universe. Base change $V\mapsto Z\times_WV$ is continuous, defines the canonical ringed-topos morphism of $u$, and identifies an etale map with slice localization. The chart-adjunction realization identifies the module functors in the statement with these ringed-topos functors, preserving their units. Apply the ringed-site derived-image existence theorem to this continuous functor and structural ring map: its inverse image on set sheaves is left exact because it is a geometric morphism. It gives total derived tensor pullback and direct image, computed respectively on flat-term K-flat and K-injective resolutions, and their canonical adjunction; K-injective resolutions of module complexes exist on these small ringed sites, and the right-derived unit is invertible on every K-injective complex by the cited existence statement and right-derived-functor definition. The same construction applies on every slice. Transport these functors through the ringed-site equivalences to the small etale sites.

For an etale $a:V\to W$, the underived restriction lemma identifies $a^*$ with module restriction to $\mathcal C_W/V$, and identifies $b^*$ similarly. Restriction is exact by the ringed-site restriction theorem. The exact-functor derivation theorem therefore computes $La^*=a^*$ and $Lb^*=b^*$ on every representative complex, not only on a resolution. In particular $H^q(a^*L)=a^*H^q(L)$: exactness preserves the kernel and image defining this cohomology quotient. These identifications include the empty etale chart.

Represent $K$ by a K-injective complex $I$, which exists by the cited K-injective resolution statement. It computes $Ru_*K$ because the right-derived unit is invertible on K-injective complexes. Restriction of $I$ to $\mathcal C_Z/(Z\times_WV)$ is K-injective by the K-injective restriction theorem, hence by the same unit property computes $R(u_V)_*b^*K$. The underived chart comparison identifies $a^*u_*I$ and $(u_V)_*b^*I$ termwise: at any etale test space $T\to V$, both are the compatible sections of $I$ over $Z\times_WT$. Its compatibility with restrictions and module maps makes it an isomorphism of complexes. Passing to the derived category gives $a^*Ru_*K\cong R(u_V)_*b^*K$. The cited normalized slice-comparison theorem supplies naturality and compatibility with the derived adjunctions; its hypotheses hold in the enlarged site model of step 1.

Apply the common K-flat word theorem to the ringed-topos maps of the square. Choose one flat-term K-flat resolution $P\to L$. Every iterated pullback of $P$ remains flat-term K-flat. Thus the two functors $b^*Lu^*$ and $Lu_V^*a^*$ are computed by $b^*u^*P$ and $u_V^*a^*P$. The underived square comparison identifies these complexes; locally it multiplies successive scalar coefficients and keeps the restricted section. Its normalized descent gives $b^*Lu^*L\cong Lu_V^*a^*L$, naturally in $L$. This uses exactness of the etale arrows from step 2, but no flatness of $u$. The same computation compares pullback along any two equal composite paths, including a square with etale vertical scheme charts which need not be cartesian.

The local criterion for quasi-coherence follows directly from its definition by local presentations. If a module $M$ restricts to quasi-coherent modules on a jointly surjective etale scheme family $U_i\to X$, refine on each $U_i$ to objects on whose slice $M$ has a presentation by sums of structure modules. For any scheme object $T\to X$, the fibre products $T\times_XU_i$ are schemes and cover $T$. Pulling back the refining covers gives a cover of $T$; restriction of each presentation is still exact by step 2, and restriction carries a sum of structure modules to the corresponding sum on the slice (both are the sheafification of the same restricted free-module presheaf). Hence $M$ has the required local presentations on $X_{\mathrm{et}}$. Conversely such presentations restrict to every slice. Apply this equivalence to each $H^q(E)$ and use $H^q(E|_{U_i})=H^q(E)|_{U_i}$ from step 2. This proves the asserted derived quasi-coherence test for any jointly surjective scheme family.

For any scheme $T$, write $\epsilon_T:T_{\mathrm{et}}\to T_{\mathrm{Zar}}$ for the canonical ringed-site map in the ordinary comparison-square statement. Its pullback is exact on all modules. Indeed the geometric stalk formula identifies the pulled-back stalk sequence with the Zariski stalk sequence tensored with $\mathcal O_{T,x}^{\mathrm{sh}}$. Zariski stalks preserve exact sequences by the module-stalk theorem, and strict henselization is faithfully flat, hence preserves that exactness by the definition of faithful flatness. Exact scalar forgetting and exact geometric stalks identify the stalks of every homology sheaf of the pulled-back sequence with zero. Geometric-stalk conservativity makes each underlying homology sheaf zero; faithful exact forgetting then makes its module homology zero. This proves exactness without any quasi-coherence hypothesis. The exact-functor derivation theorem identifies $L\epsilon_T^*$ with termwise $\epsilon_T^*$, so $H^q(\epsilon_T^*M)=\epsilon_T^*H^q(M)$ for every derived object $M$.

Let $E\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_{T,\mathrm{et}})$ and $N^q=H^q(E)$. Take the set $\mathcal B$ of affine etale objects over $T$. Every etale scheme object has an affine open cover by the affine-basis theorem. For $U\in\mathcal B$, restriction of $N^q$ is quasi-coherent by its local-presentation definition (or step 5). The ordinary Zariski-etale QCoh equivalence writes this restriction as $F_{\mathrm{et}}$ for a quasi-coherent Zariski module $F$ on $U$. The site-localization theorem identifies the slice with $U_{\mathrm{et}}$. Affine etale acyclicity gives $H^p(U_{\mathrm{et}},F_{\mathrm{et}})=0$ for $p>0$, and the module-derived-evaluation/slice comparison gives the same vanishing for module-derived evaluation. Its enough-injectives hypothesis follows from the K-injective-resolution theorem: resolving $M[0]$ embeds $M$ in the injective degree-zero term, since a zero image has zero cohomology class. An injective resolution of $N^q$ is a bounded-below complex of injectives, hence K-injective by the cited bounded-below theorem, so it represents $N^q[0]$ in $R\Gamma(U,-)$ and $H^p(R\Gamma(U,N^q[0]))$ is the vanishing module-derived evaluation. The acyclic-basis theorem now gives canonical edge isomorphisms $H^q(R\Gamma(U,E))\cong N^q(U)$ for all $q\in\mathbf Z$, natural under restriction between affine etale objects. No boundedness is required.

proof.text: Choose $E\to I$ K-injective. The direct-image description in the ordinary comparison-square statement says $\epsilon_{T,*}I(W)=I(W)$ for an open $W\subset T$. It computes $R\epsilon_{T,*}E$ in the canonical derived adjunction. It is also K-injective: by adjunction, including homotopies, maps from an acyclic $A$ to $\epsilon_{T,*}I$ correspond to maps from the acyclic $\epsilon_T^*A$ to $I$, which are null-homotopic. Exact presheaf-module sheafification says $H^q(\epsilon_{T,*}I)$ is the sheafification of $W\mapsto H^q(I(W))$. On affine opens the preceding step identifies this with $W\mapsto N^q(W)$, compatibly with restrictions. Thus $H^q(R\epsilon_{T,*}E)\cong\epsilon_{T,*}N^q$, which is quasi-coherent by the ordinary QCoh equivalence. Set $M=R\epsilon_{T,*}E$. The cohomology map of the canonical derived counit $\epsilon_T^*M\to E$ is the ordinary counit $\epsilon_T^*\epsilon_{T,*}N^q\to N^q$: on affine etale objects the preceding edge map takes a cycle of $I(U)$ to its local cohomology section, and counit evaluation multiplies the pulled-back section by its scalar; boundaries map to boundaries. These are precisely the ordinary tensor counit formulas. The ordinary QCoh equivalence makes this counit invertible. Exactness from step 6 therefore makes the derived counit an isomorphism. In particular every such $E$ is $\epsilon_T^*M$ for a Zariski quasi-coherent derived object $M$.

proof.text: For a scheme morphism $h:U\to V$, the ordinary comparison-square theorem gives $\epsilon_U^*h^*\cong h_{\mathrm{et}}^*\epsilon_V^*$ on all Zariski modules, with the specified scalar actions. Apply the common K-flat word theorem to these two words of ringed pullbacks. On one flat-term K-flat resolution $P\to M$, both iterated pullbacks remain flat-term K-flat and the ordinary comparison gives an isomorphism of their representative complexes. Its normalized descent is $\epsilon_U^*Lh_{\mathrm{Zar}}^*M\cong Lh_{\mathrm{et}}^*\epsilon_V^*M$, where step 6 identifies the derived $\epsilon^*$ with exact pullback. If $M$ has quasi-coherent cohomology, the scheme derived-pullback theorem gives quasi-coherent cohomology for $Lh_{\mathrm{Zar}}^*M$. The ordinary QCoh equivalence and exactness in step 6 show that its $\epsilon_U^*$ image also has quasi-coherent cohomology. This comparison requires neither qcqs hypotheses on $h$ nor a direct-image comparison.

proof.text: Let $L\in D_{\mathrm{QCoh}}(\mathcal O_W)$. Choose a surjective etale scheme chart $a:V\to W$ and then a surjective etale scheme chart $U\to Z\times_WV$. Base change and composition of surjective etale morphisms show that $c:U\to Z$ is surjective etale; the induced $h:U\to V$ is a scheme morphism with $u c=a h$. These assertions use the atlas in the definition of algebraic space and the cited fibre-product and etale-permanence statements. Step 4 gives $c^*Lu^*L\cong Lh_{\mathrm{et}}^*a^*L$. By step 5, $a^*L$ has quasi-coherent cohomology. Apply step 8 to write $a^*L\cong\epsilon_V^*M$ with $M$ having Zariski quasi-coherent cohomology. Step 9 identifies its derived pullback with $\epsilon_U^*Lh_{\mathrm{Zar}}^*M$ and proves quasi-coherence of its cohomology. The cover criterion in step 5 concludes that $Lu^*L$ has quasi-coherent cohomology. The fibre product $Z\times_WV$ need not be a scheme, which is why the further chart $U$ was chosen.

source.place: Tag 08F4 (lemma-quasi-coherence-pullback), with the scheme comparison established in steps 6-9.

proof.text: For any composable string of space morphisms, use the ordinary ringed composition and unit comparisons, including their structural ring maps, from the enlarged model. On one common flat-term K-flat resolution these are the ordinary iterated tensor-pullback maps. The common K-flat word theorem descends their associativity and unit equalities, so the derived pullbacks have the claimed canonical coherent comparisons. Define the pushforward comparison as the right-adjoint conjugate of the pullback comparison for the composite adjunctions of step 1. Conjugation takes isomorphisms to isomorphisms, reverses composition, and preserves identities, so these right comparisons obey the same coherence laws. The unit equation in the adjoint-uniqueness theorem fixes the comparison uniquely; its adjoint is the counit equation. Thus the comparisons preserve the specified units and counits. In the etale square the normalized slice theorem of step 3 identifies the direct-image comparison with this adjunction-compatible normalization.
